prompt: What is a Database?

options.text: An organized collection of logically interrelated data
A software program that writes C code

explanation: A database is an organized, integrated collection of logically related data models designed to meet the information needs of an organization.

prompt: What is the primary drawback of traditional File Processing Systems compared to a DBMS?

options.text: Data redundancy, data inconsistency, and data isolation

explanation: File systems suffer from redundant data storage across multiple files, leading to update anomalies and inconsistent data.

prompt: What is the Three-Schema Architecture also known as?
explanation: The ANSI/SPARC 3-tier architecture divides database descriptions into External, Conceptual, and Internal levels to achieve data independence.

prompt: Which level of the ANSI-SPARC architecture describes how data is physically stored on hardware storage media?
explanation: The Internal (Physical) level describes the physical storage structure, access paths, block organizations, and indexing techniques.

prompt: Which level of the ANSI-SPARC architecture describes what data is stored and the relationships among data for the entire community of users?
explanation: The Conceptual (logical) level provides a unified global representation of all entities, data types, relationships, and constraints.

prompt: Which level of the ANSI-SPARC architecture provides customized views tailored for individual user groups?
explanation: The External level describes the individual views of different end-users, hiding irrelevant portions of the database.

prompt: What is Physical Data Independence?

options.text: The ability to modify the conceptual schema without altering external views
The ability to modify the physical storage structures or access paths without altering the conceptual schema

explanation: Physical data independence insulates the conceptual schema from changes in disk storage, indexing, or physical file reorganization.

prompt: What is Logical Data Independence?

options.text: The ability to alter the physical disk format
The ability to modify the conceptual schema without having to rewrite external schemas and application programs
Running queries on the CPU cache

explanation: Logical data independence allows adding new entities or expanding attributes at the conceptual level without breaking existing user views.

prompt: Which type of data independence is generally more difficult to achieve?
explanation: Logical data independence is harder because application programs are tightly coupled to the logical structure of the data they access.

prompt: Who is the Database Administrator (DBA)?

options.text: An end-user who enters daily data
A person/team with central control over data, schema definition, security policies, and performance tuning
A programmer who writes web CSS

explanation: The DBA coordinates and manages the database, schema definitions, access privileges, backup/recovery, and performance optimization.

prompt: Which of the following is a core responsibility of a DBA?

options.text: Authorizing database access privileges and establishing backup/recovery procedures

explanation: DBA duties include schema definition, user authorization/security, backup, crash recovery, and storage monitoring.

prompt: Which class of database users interacts with the system solely through canned, pre-written application interfaces (e.g., bank tellers, ticket booking agents)?
explanation: Naive (parametric) users access the database through menu-driven graphical applications without knowing SQL or database structure.

prompt: Which class of database users writes ad-hoc queries directly in query languages (like SQL) to analyze data?
explanation: Sophisticated users (engineers, analysts, scientists) interact with the DBMS using interactive query tools without written programs.

prompt: What is the Data Dictionary (System Catalog)?

options.text: A standard English dictionary for spelling checks
A special database containing metadata (data about data), schemas, constraints, and user authorizations
A collection of temporary log files

explanation: The data dictionary stores metadata including table definitions, column types, integrity constraints, indexes, and user permissions.

prompt: In a Hierarchical Data Model, how are data relationships organized?

options.text: As a collection of tables and relations
As an arbitrary graph with many-to-many pointers

explanation: The hierarchical model represents data as tree structures where each child record has exactly one parent record.

prompt: In a Network Data Model, how are records related?

options.text: A child record can have multiple parent records (many-to-many graph)

explanation: The network model (CODASYL) allows a child node (member) to have multiple parent nodes (owners), forming complex graphs.

prompt: Who proposed the Relational Data Model in 1970?
explanation: Dr. E.F. Codd published the relational model in 1970 at IBM, representing data as mathematical relations (tables).

prompt: What is a Front-End tool in database applications?

options.text: The physical SATA hard drive controller
An application software or graphical interface that enables users to query, display, and manipulate data

explanation: Front-end tools (e.g., web portals, reporting tools, forms) interact with end-users and communicate with the back-end DBMS engine.

prompt: Which component of the DBMS engine is responsible for executing disk reads and managing memory buffers?
explanation: The Storage Manager interfaces with the operating system file system to allocate disk space and manage memory caching buffers.

prompt: What is Metadata?

options.text: Data that contains confidential financial secrets
Data about data describing structure, types, and constraints

explanation: Metadata describes the schema, structure, data types, constraints, and access rights of the underlying stored data.

prompt: What is Data Redundancy?

options.text: Storing duplicate copies of the same data across multiple files

explanation: Redundancy refers to unnecessary duplication of identical data across several storage locations.

prompt: What is Data Inconsistency?

options.text: When different copies of the same data show conflicting values due to partial updates

explanation: Inconsistency arises when redundant data is updated in one location but not in another.

prompt: Which language is used by the DBA to define database schema structures and tables?
explanation: DDL statements (CREATE, ALTER, DROP) define and modify database structures.

prompt: Which language is used to retrieve and update data in database relations?
explanation: DML statements (SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE) query and manipulate data records.

prompt: A database schema is defined as:

options.text: The overall logical design and structure of the database
The collection of actual data stored at a particular moment
A single row in a table

explanation: The schema is the invariant structural blueprint of the database.

prompt: What is a Database Instance (or State)?

options.text: The collection of actual data stored in the database at a specific point in time

explanation: The database state or instance represents the snapshot of actual data at any given moment.

prompt: What is the mapping between the External and Conceptual schemas responsible for?
explanation: External-Conceptual mapping maps individual user views to global logical tables, providing logical data independence.

prompt: What is the mapping between the Conceptual and Internal schemas responsible for?
explanation: Conceptual-Internal mapping maps global tables to physical storage blocks and files, ensuring physical data independence.

prompt: Which of the following is an example of an open-source Relational DBMS?
explanation: MySQL and PostgreSQL are prominent open-source relational database management systems.

prompt: In client-server database architecture, where does the DBMS database engine reside?
explanation: The database engine runs on the central server machine, processing queries submitted by client applications.

prompt: What is Query Optimization?

options.text: Choosing the most efficient physical execution plan for an incoming SQL query

explanation: The query optimizer evaluates alternative execution strategies to minimize disk I/O and processing time.

prompt: Which of the following is NOT a relational DBMS?
explanation: MongoDB is a document-oriented NoSQL database, not a traditional relational DBMS.

prompt: What is the primary role of the Transaction Manager in a DBMS?

options.text: Ensuring transactions preserve ACID properties and handling commits/rollbacks

explanation: The transaction manager coordinates transaction states, guarantees ACID properties, and maintains data consistency.

prompt: What is the Concurrency Control Manager responsible for?

options.text: Controlling multiple users updating the database simultaneously to prevent conflicts

explanation: Concurrency control ensures multiple interleaved transactions do not leave the database in an inconsistent state.

prompt: What does the DDL Compiler produce?

options.text: A set of metadata tables stored in the Data Dictionary

explanation: The DDL compiler processes schema declarations and writes corresponding schema metadata into the system catalog.

prompt: Which of the following describes an Application Programmer user class?

options.text: Developers who write application programs that interact with the DBMS using embedded SQL or APIs

explanation: Application programmers develop software interfaces and write business logic using database APIs.

prompt: In a distributed DBMS, where is data located?

options.text: On a single central server exclusively

explanation: A distributed DBMS manages data physically distributed across multiple interconnected computer nodes.

prompt: Which model represents data as entities, attributes, and relationships?
explanation: The Entity-Relationship model conceptualizes data as real-world entities having attributes and interrelationships.

prompt: What is a View in a database?

options.text: A physical copy of table records on disk
A virtual table derived from the result of an underlying SQL query

explanation: A view contains no physical stored rows; it dynamically computes data from underlying base tables upon query execution.

prompt: What is Data Integrity?

options.text: The accuracy, consistency, and correctness of stored data enforced by constraints
The physical weight of the storage disk
The speed of the network router

explanation: Data integrity guarantees that data conforms to all defined business rules and structural constraints.

prompt: Which integrity rule states that no component of a primary key can be NULL?
explanation: Entity integrity ensures that every tuple has a distinct, fully defined identity via its non-null primary key.

prompt: Which constraint ensures values in a column belong to a permitted set of valid atomic values?
explanation: Domain constraints enforce valid data types, formats, ranges, and allowed values for an attribute.

prompt: What does the term 'Enterprise' refer to in database context?

options.text: A commercial organization whose operational information is modeled in a database

explanation: In database engineering, enterprise refers to the business, university, hospital, or company whose data is managed.

prompt: Why is centralized database control beneficial for an organization?

options.text: It enforces standards, minimizes redundancy, ensures security, and maintains consistent data
It eliminates the need for software

explanation: Centralized control enables consistent policy enforcement, uniform data naming, coordinated backups, and security.

prompt: Which language level is SQL classified as?
explanation: SQL is a declarative language: users specify *what* data to retrieve rather than *how* algorithms step through files.

prompt: What is an ad-hoc query?

options.text: A spontaneous, unplanned query created on the spot by a user to answer a specific question

explanation: Ad-hoc queries are dynamically typed queries created as-needed by analysts to inspect data.

prompt: What happens during a Database Crash Recovery process?

options.text: The recovery manager uses transaction log files to REDO committed changes and UNDO uncommitted operations
The database is converted to Excel

explanation: Crash recovery brings the database to a consistent state by replaying committed transactions and rolling back incomplete ones.

prompt: What is an Access Path in physical DBMS design?

options.text: The physical URL of a web server
The physical data structure (e.g., B-Tree index or hash index) used to efficiently locate records on disk

explanation: An access path specifies indexing structures and disk organization utilized by the query engine to read tuples.

prompt: What is the primary role of the Buffer Pool in a DBMS?

options.text: Temporary RAM area caching disk pages to avoid slow physical disk reads

explanation: Buffer pools cache frequently accessed table blocks in fast RAM, minimizing expensive disk I/O.

prompt: Which ANSI-SPARC level is completely hidden from ordinary application end-users?
explanation: The physical internal level (block layouts, byte offsets, indexing structures) is completely hidden from application users.

prompt: Who introduced the Entity-Relationship (E-R) model in 1976?
explanation: Dr. Peter Chen introduced the E-R model in his seminal 1976 paper 'The Entity-Relationship Model: Toward a Unified View of Data'.

prompt: What is an Entity in the E-R model?

options.text: A real-world object or concept that is distinguishable from other objects

explanation: An entity is an independent thing or object in the real world (e.g., an employee, a student, a car) that has identity.

prompt: In an E-R diagram, which geometric symbol represents an Entity Set?
explanation: Rectangles represent strong entity sets in standard Chen notation.

prompt: In an E-R diagram, which geometric symbol represents a Relationship Set?
explanation: Diamonds denote relationships that connect two or more participating entity sets.

prompt: In an E-R diagram, which geometric symbol represents an Attribute?
explanation: Attributes are depicted as ovals (ellipses) connected to their respective entity rectangle.

prompt: How is a Key Attribute (Primary Key) represented in an E-R diagram?

options.text: An ellipse with its attribute name underlined with a solid line

explanation: A primary key attribute is denoted by underlining its text inside the attribute ellipse.

prompt: What is a Multivalued Attribute?

options.text: An attribute that has only one value for an entity
An attribute that can take multiple values for a single entity instance (e.g., PhoneNumbers, Skills)
An attribute that cannot be null
An attribute composed of other attributes

explanation: Multivalued attributes can store a set of values for a single entity, such as multiple phone numbers or degrees.

prompt: How is a Multivalued Attribute represented in an E-R diagram?
explanation: A double oval (concentric ellipses) denotes a multivalued attribute.

prompt: What is a Composite Attribute?

options.text: An attribute that can be divided into smaller sub-components (e.g., Name into FirstName and LastName)
An attribute that holds binary numbers
A primary key with two words

explanation: Composite attributes (like Address = Street, City, State, Pin) are composed of simpler, independent sub-attributes.

prompt: What is a Derived Attribute?

options.text: An attribute physically stored on hard disk
An attribute whose value is computed dynamically from other related attributes (e.g., Age derived from DateOfBirth)

explanation: Derived attributes are not physically stored; they are calculated on demand from stored attributes.

prompt: How is a Derived Attribute represented in an E-R diagram?
explanation: Dashed or dotted ovals represent derived attributes in Chen notation.

prompt: What is a Weak Entity in the E-R model?

options.text: An entity that cannot be stored on disk
An entity that does not possess sufficient attributes to form its own primary key and depends on an identifying owner entity
An entity with only one attribute

explanation: A weak entity cannot be uniquely identified by its own attributes alone and relies on an identifying relationship with an owner entity.

prompt: How is a Weak Entity Set represented in an E-R diagram?
explanation: Double rectangles depict weak entity sets, emphasizing their dependency on an identifying strong entity.

prompt: How is an Identifying Relationship Set (connecting weak entity to owner) represented?
explanation: Double diamonds represent identifying relationships associated with weak entity sets.

prompt: What is the discriminator (partial key) of a weak entity set?

options.text: The foreign key of the database
A set of attributes that distinguishes among all entities of the weak entity set belonging to the same owner entity

explanation: The partial key uniquely distinguishes weak entity instances associated with the same parent owner entity.

prompt: How is the Partial Key of a weak entity represented in an E-R diagram?
explanation: A dashed (dotted) underline under the attribute name denotes a partial key.

prompt: What is Cardinality Ratio (Mapping Cardinality) in a binary relationship?

options.text: The number of bytes in each record
The number of entity instances to which another entity instance can be associated via a relationship set
The number of tables in the database

explanation: Mapping cardinalities express whether a relationship is One-to-One (1:1), One-to-Many (1:N), Many-to-One (N:1), or Many-to-Many (M:N).

prompt: A department has one manager, and each manager manages one department. This relationship is an example of:
explanation: Since each department pairs with at most one manager and vice-versa, this is a 1:1 relationship.

prompt: One teacher teaches multiple courses, and each course is taught by only one teacher. This is a:
explanation: From teacher to courses, the mapping is One-to-Many (1:N).

prompt: A student can enroll in multiple courses, and a course can have multiple students enrolled. This is a:
explanation: Since students and courses share multi-way associations, the relationship is Many-to-Many (M:N).

prompt: What is Total Participation (Existence Dependency) in an E-R relationship?

options.text: Every entity in the entity set must participate in at least one relationship instance

explanation: Total participation requires that every entity in the set exists in the relationship (indicated by double lines).

prompt: How is Total Participation represented in an E-R diagram?

options.text: Double line connecting entity to relationship

explanation: Double lines signify total participation; single lines indicate partial participation.

prompt: What is Partial Participation?

options.text: Only some entities in the entity set participate in the relationship instances

explanation: In partial participation, some entities in the set may not participate in the relationship.

prompt: What is a Recursive (Unary) Relationship?

options.text: A relationship where the same entity set participates more than once in different roles (e.g., Employee MANAGES Employee)
A relationship between three different tables

explanation: In a recursive relationship, entities of the same entity set relate to each other under distinct roles.

prompt: When mapping a Many-to-Many (M:N) relationship to relational tables, what is required?

options.text: Adding a foreign key column to one table
Creating a new distinct junction (bridge) table containing foreign keys from both participating tables
Combining both tables into a single column

explanation: An M:N relationship cannot be represented inside either base table; it requires a new junction relation.

prompt: What forms the Primary Key of the junction table created from an M:N relationship without attributes?

options.text: The primary key of entity 1 only
The combination (composite key) of the primary keys of both participating entity sets

explanation: The composite combination of the foreign keys of both entities forms the primary key of the junction table.

prompt: When mapping a 1:N relationship from Entity A (1) to Entity B (N), how is the relationship represented?

options.text: By adding the primary key of A as a Foreign Key in table B
By adding the primary key of B as a Foreign Key in table A

explanation: In 1:N relationships, the primary key of the 'one' side is embedded as a foreign key on the 'many' side (table B).

prompt: When mapping a Weak Entity Set to a relational table, what constitutes its primary key?

options.text: The partial key combined with the primary key of the identifying owner entity
It cannot have a primary key

explanation: The primary key of a weak entity table consists of the owner entity's primary key plus the weak entity's partial key.

prompt: What is Specialization in Extended E-R (EER) modeling?

options.text: Top-down process of designing sub-groupings within an entity set based on distinguishing features

explanation: Specialization defines sub-classes from a generalized super-class using a top-down design strategy.

prompt: What is Generalization in EER modeling?

options.text: Bottom-up process of extracting common attributes among multiple entities into a higher-level super-class

explanation: Generalization synthesizes multiple entity types that share common features into a single generalized entity.

prompt: What is Aggregation in EER modeling?

options.text: An abstraction through which relationships are treated as higher-level entities to participate in further relationships

explanation: Aggregation allows treating an existing relationship between entities as an abstract entity for higher-order relationships.

prompt: In an E-R diagram, what does an arrow from a relationship to an entity set represent?

options.text: A cardinality constraint of at most 1 (one-side)

explanation: An arrow directed toward an entity set indicates that an entity participates at most once (mapping cardinality 1).

prompt: What is the degree of a Ternary relationship?
explanation: A ternary relationship involves three distinct participating entity sets.

prompt: What is an Entity Set?

options.text: A collection of entities of the same type that share the same attributes

explanation: An entity set is a collection (set) of all entities sharing identical attribute structures (e.g., all Students).

prompt: Can an entity set have more than one candidate key?

options.text: No, only one key is allowed
Yes, an entity set can have multiple candidate keys from which one is chosen as primary
Only if it is a weak entity

explanation: An entity set may possess multiple candidate keys (e.g., RollNo, AadharNo, Email), one of which becomes the primary key.

prompt: What is an Atomic Attribute?

options.text: An attribute that cannot be divided into sub-parts
An attribute composed of radioactive data

explanation: Atomic (simple) attributes represent indivisible scalar values like age, salary, or percentage.

prompt: What is a Stored Attribute?

options.text: An attribute whose value is physically saved in the database

explanation: Stored attributes are persisted directly on storage media, unlike derived attributes.

prompt: In an E-R diagram for a hospital, 'Patient HAS Doctor' is an example of:
explanation: 'HAS' connects the Patient entity set and Doctor entity set as a relationship set.

prompt: What happens to weak entity records when their identifying owner entity instance is deleted?

options.text: They are cascade deleted (or orphaned violation occurs)

explanation: Because weak entities depend on owner existence, deleting the owner entity deletes associated weak entities (ON DELETE CASCADE).

prompt: Can a relationship set possess attributes of its own (descriptive attributes)?

options.text: Yes, descriptive attributes can record information specific to the association (e.g., DateOfAppointment)

explanation: Descriptive attributes belong to the relationship itself (e.g., Grade in a Student TAKES Course relationship).

prompt: When mapping a 1:1 relationship where both sides have total participation, what is the best strategy?

options.text: Merge both entity sets into a single unified relational table

explanation: When both sides have total participation, combining them into one table avoids nulls and optimizes joins.

prompt: Which notation depicts roles played by entities in a recursive relationship?

options.text: Labeling the connecting lines with role names (e.g., 'manager', 'worker')

explanation: Role indicators label the relationship lines to clarify roles played by members of the same entity set.

prompt: What is the primary goal of conceptual database design using E-R modeling?

options.text: Creating a high-level, implementation-independent semantic representation of organizational data

explanation: Conceptual design produces an enterprise-wide model of data requirements free of DBMS software constraints.

prompt: A composite attribute is mapped to a relational table by:

options.text: Flattening it by including only its individual atomic sub-attributes as separate columns
Storing it in a text file

explanation: Relational 1NF requires atomic values; composite attributes are flattened into their leaf sub-attributes.

prompt: A multivalued attribute is mapped to a relational table by:

options.text: Creating a new separate table containing the attribute value and the parent entity's primary key

explanation: Multivalued attributes violate 1NF if stored in the parent table, requiring a separate table with a composite key.

prompt: In an E-R diagram, how is disjoint constraint in specialization represented?
explanation: The letter 'd' indicates disjoint specialization (an entity can belong to at most one sub-class).

prompt: In EER modeling, what does overlapping specialization ('o') mean?

options.text: An entity can simultaneously belong to multiple sub-classes
An entity belongs to zero sub-classes

explanation: Overlapping ('o') permits an entity instance (e.g., an Employee who is both an Author and a Reviewer) to be in multiple subclasses.

prompt: What is an Identifying Entity in weak entity terminology?

options.text: The owner entity whose primary key identifies the weak entity

explanation: The identifying entity (owner entity) provides identity to the dependent weak entity.

prompt: What type of relationship exists between an Invoice and its LineItems?

options.text: Strong entity to Weak entity identifying relationship (1:N)

explanation: LineItems cannot exist without the parent Invoice and use ItemNumber as a partial key, making it a weak entity.

prompt: Which phase of database design immediately follows requirements analysis?
explanation: Requirements analysis leads directly to conceptual schema design via E-R modeling.

prompt: In relational database terminology, a row in a table is formally known as a:
explanation: In formal relational algebra, a row is called a Tuple, representing a single record.

prompt: In relational database terminology, a column in a table is formally known as an:
explanation: A column corresponds to an Attribute, representing a specific property or field of the entity.

prompt: What is the Degree of a relation in relational algebra?

options.text: The total number of rows (tuples) in the relation
The total number of columns (attributes) in the relation

explanation: The degree (or arity) of a relation is the number of attributes (columns) it possesses.

prompt: What is the Cardinality of a relation?

options.text: The total number of tuples (rows) currently in the relation

explanation: Cardinality is the total count of tuples (rows) currently stored in the relation.

prompt: What is a Domain in relational model?

options.text: The set of all permissible atomic values for an attribute

explanation: A domain is the pool of legal, atomic values that an attribute is allowed to take.

prompt: What does the Entity Integrity Constraint state?

options.text: A foreign key cannot be null
No primary key attribute (or component of a composite primary key) can have a NULL value
Every table must have at least 10 rows

explanation: Entity integrity ensures every tuple has a distinct identity; hence, primary key components cannot be NULL.

prompt: What does the Referential Integrity Constraint state?

options.text: A foreign key value in a referencing relation must either match a valid primary key value in the referenced relation, or be NULL

explanation: Referential integrity prevents orphaned records by enforcing valid relationships between referencing and referenced tables.

prompt: In a Foreign Key constraint, what does ON DELETE CASCADE specify?

options.text: Deletion of the parent row is blocked if matching child rows exist
When a parent row in the referenced table is deleted, all matching child rows in the referencing table are automatically deleted
Child foreign keys are set to NULL
Child foreign keys are set to 0

explanation: CASCADE automatically propagates deletions from the primary key table to all dependent foreign key rows.

prompt: In a Foreign Key constraint, what does ON DELETE RESTRICT (or NO ACTION) specify?

options.text: The DBMS rejects and aborts the deletion of the parent row if any child rows reference it

explanation: RESTRICT prevents parent deletion as long as active referencing rows exist, preserving integrity.

prompt: What is a Functional Dependency X -> Y?

options.text: A constraint stating that if two tuples agree on attribute set X, they must also agree on attribute set Y
A foreign key between X and Y

explanation: X -> Y means X uniquely determines Y: identical X values across two tuples guarantee identical Y values.

prompt: A Functional Dependency X -> Y is called Trivial if:

options.text: Y is a subset of X (Y ⊆ X)
X and Y are completely disjoint

explanation: A trivial functional dependency is one that always holds automatically because the right-hand side is already contained in the left-hand side (e.g., {RollNo, Name} -> RollNo).

prompt: Which set of inference rules is sound and complete for deriving all functional dependencies implied by a set of FDs?
explanation: Armstrong's Axioms (Reflexivity, Augmentation, Transitivity) form a sound and complete basis for reasoning about functional dependencies.

prompt: Armstrong's Transitivity Rule states that:

options.text: If X -> Y and Y -> Z, then X -> Z
If X -> Y, then XZ -> YZ
If Y ⊆ X, then X -> Y
If X -> Y and X -> Z, then X -> YZ

explanation: Transitivity allows chaining functional dependencies: X uniquely determining Y and Y uniquely determining Z implies X determines Z.

prompt: What is the Closure of an attribute set X (denoted X+)?

options.text: The number of characters in X
The set of all attributes that are functionally determined by X under a given set of FDs

explanation: The attribute closure X+ includes all attributes whose values can be uniquely deduced from X using known FDs.

prompt: An attribute set K is a Candidate Key for relation R if:

options.text: K+ contains all attributes of R, and no proper subset of K has this property (minimal superkey)

explanation: A candidate key is a minimal superkey: it uniquely determines every attribute in R without redundant columns.

prompt: What is an Update (Modification) Anomaly?

options.text: When inserting data takes more than 1 second
When updating data in one place leaves conflicting, inconsistent values in un-updated redundant copies
When a computer updates its OS

explanation: Update anomalies occur when redundant data requires updating multiple rows; missing any row causes data inconsistency.

prompt: What is a Deletion Anomaly?

options.text: Deleting a row accidentally causes unintended loss of entirely different, valuable information
Deleting a row takes too long
Hard disk runs out of space

explanation: A deletion anomaly occurs when deleting one fact inadvertently deletes other distinct, unrelated information (e.g., deleting the last student enrolled deletes course info).

prompt: What is an Insertion Anomaly?

options.text: The inability to record certain facts without artificially adding unrelated dummy data

explanation: An insertion anomaly happens when new data cannot be recorded unless unrelated data is also present (e.g., cannot add a new course without enrolling a student).

prompt: What is the requirement for a relation to be in First Normal Form (1NF)?

options.text: All attributes must contain only atomic (indivisible) values, and there are no repeating groups or multivalued attributes
Every non-prime attribute is fully dependent on the primary key

explanation: 1NF mandates flat, atomic domain values in every cell, prohibiting arrays, lists, or repeating attribute groups.

prompt: What is the requirement for a relation to be in Second Normal Form (2NF)?

options.text: It is in 1NF and contains no transitive dependencies
It is in 1NF and contains NO Partial Dependencies (every non-prime attribute is fully functionally dependent on the whole candidate key)
Every determinant is a candidate key

explanation: 2NF eliminates partial dependencies: no non-prime attribute can be determined by a proper subset of a composite candidate key.

prompt: What is a Partial Functional Dependency?

options.text: A dependency where a non-prime attribute is determined by only a part of a composite candidate key
A dependency where the key is half empty
A foreign key that is null

explanation: Partial dependency occurs when A -> B, where A is a proper subset of a candidate key and B is non-prime.

prompt: What is the requirement for a relation to be in Third Normal Form (3NF)?

options.text: It is in 2NF and contains NO Transitive Dependencies for non-prime attributes

explanation: 3NF requires that for every non-trivial FD X -> Y, either X is a superkey or Y is a prime attribute (eliminating transitive dependencies).

prompt: What is a Transitive Dependency?

options.text: When X -> Y and Y -> Z (where Y is not a candidate key), resulting in indirect dependency X -> Z
A dependency that transfers across network cables
A foreign key to another server

explanation: A transitive dependency occurs when non-key attribute X determines non-key attribute Y, which in turn determines non-key attribute Z.

prompt: What is Boyce-Codd Normal Form (BCNF)?

options.text: A stricter version of 3NF where for EVERY non-trivial functional dependency X -> Y, X MUST be a Superkey
A form that allows repeating groups
A normal form for binary trees

explanation: BCNF is stricter than 3NF: it requires the left-hand determinant of every non-trivial FD to be a superkey, with no exceptions.

prompt: Can a relation in 3NF violate BCNF?

options.text: Yes, when a relation has multiple overlapping composite candidate keys
Only if it has zero rows

explanation: A relation with overlapping candidate keys can satisfy 3NF (because Y is prime) while violating BCNF (because X is not a superkey).

prompt: What is a Prime Attribute?

options.text: An attribute that is an odd prime number
An attribute that is a member of ANY candidate key of the relation
The first column of a table

explanation: A prime attribute is any attribute that belongs to at least one candidate key of the relation.

prompt: What is a Non-Prime Attribute?

options.text: An attribute that is not a member of any candidate key

explanation: Non-prime attributes are those attributes that do not belong to any candidate key.

prompt: If a relation has only simple (single-attribute) candidate keys and is in 1NF, is it automatically in 2NF?

options.text: Yes, because partial dependencies can only exist with composite keys
No, it must be normalized further

explanation: Partial dependencies require a proper subset of a candidate key; single-attribute keys have no proper non-empty subsets, so 2NF holds automatically.

prompt: What is the primary objective of Database Normalization?

options.text: Minimizing data redundancy and avoiding update, insertion, and deletion anomalies
Increasing the number of foreign keys

explanation: Normalization decomposes relations systematically to reduce redundancy and maintain data integrity without losing information.

prompt: What is a Lossless-Join Decomposition?

options.text: A decomposition where joining the decomposed relations guarantees recovering the exact original relation without spurious tuples
A decomposition that loses half the rows

explanation: Lossless join decomposition ensures R1 ⨝ R2 = R, preventing false (spurious) data from being introduced.

prompt: For a decomposition of R into R1 and R2 to be lossless, what condition must hold?

options.text: R1 ∩ R2 must be a superkey of R1 or a superkey of R2
R1 and R2 must have zero attributes in common
R1 must have more rows than R2

explanation: The common attributes between R1 and R2 must form a superkey of at least one of the decomposed relations.

prompt: What is Dependency Preservation in relational decomposition?

options.text: All functional dependencies in original relation R can be checked by inspecting individual decomposed relations without performing joins

explanation: Dependency preservation guarantees that enforcing FDs on individual tables enforces all original constraints without costly cross-table joins.

prompt: Which normal form guarantees both Lossless-Join and Dependency Preservation always?
explanation: 3NF decompositions can always achieve both lossless-join and dependency preservation; BCNF cannot always preserve dependencies.

prompt: Consider R(A, B, C) with FD: A -> B, B -> C. Primary key is A. What normal form is R in?

options.text: 2NF (violates 3NF due to transitive dependency B -> C)

explanation: Candidate key is A. All non-prime attributes (B, C) depend on full key A (satisfies 2NF). But B -> C is a transitive dependency, violating 3NF.

prompt: To convert R(A, B, C) with A -> B, B -> C into 3NF, how should it be decomposed?
explanation: Decomposing into R1(A, B) with key A and R2(B, C) with key B eliminates the transitive dependency and satisfies 3NF.

prompt: In relation R(A, B, C, D) with FDs {AB -> C, C -> D, D -> A}, what are the candidate keys?
explanation: Computing closures: (AB)+ = ABCD; (BC)+ = BC->D->A = ABCD; (BD)+ = BD->A->C = ABCD. Candidate keys are AB, BC, BD.

prompt: What is Multi-Valued Dependency (MVD) associated with?
explanation: 4NF addresses multi-valued dependencies (X ->-> Y) where independent multi-valued facts are mixed in a single relation.

prompt: What does Fifth Normal Form (5NF / Project-Join Normal Form) deal with?
explanation: 5NF decomposes relations that cannot be reconstructed without loss from fewer than three projections (Join Dependencies).

prompt: Can a NULL value be compared to another NULL value using the equality operator (=) in SQL?

options.text: No, comparisons with NULL evaluate to UNKNOWN (Three-Valued Logic)
It causes a compiler syntax error

explanation: In SQL three-valued logic, NULL = NULL evaluates to UNKNOWN, requiring the IS NULL operator for comparison.

prompt: What does the SQL predicate 'IS NOT NULL' test for?

options.text: Whether a column contains a non-missing, defined value
Whether a row is a primary key

explanation: IS NOT NULL checks that a column contains a valid value rather than an unknown/missing NULL indicator.

prompt: What is a Surrogate Key?

options.text: A natural key derived from real-world data like Social Security Number
An artificial, system-generated unique identifier (e.g., auto-increment integer or UUID) with no business meaning
A foreign key to an external database

explanation: Surrogate keys are synthetic primary keys created by the DBMS to uniquely identify records without relying on business attributes.

prompt: What is a Natural Key?

options.text: A candidate key composed of attributes that already exist naturally in the real-world domain (e.g., PassportNumber, ISBN)

explanation: Natural keys exist in the real world and inherently carry business meaning.

prompt: What is a Composite Primary Key?

options.text: A primary key composed of two or more attributes
A primary key with multiple data types
A primary key linked to two databases

explanation: A composite primary key requires combining multiple columns to uniquely identify each tuple in a relation.

prompt: What is Denormalization?

options.text: A mistake made during database creation
The deliberate introduction of redundancy into a normalized database to optimize read performance and reduce expensive joins

explanation: Denormalization intentionally adds redundant data to high-traffic tables to improve read query performance in analytical systems.

prompt: Under which scenario is denormalization most commonly practiced?
explanation: Data warehouses and reporting systems denormalize schemas into star/snowflake schemas to accelerate complex analytical queries.

prompt: What is an orphaned record?

options.text: A child table row whose foreign key references a non-existent parent primary key

explanation: Orphaned records occur when referential integrity is violated, leaving foreign key values pointing to deleted parent entities.

prompt: What is a Superkey?

options.text: A set of one or more attributes that collectively uniquely identify a tuple in a relation

explanation: A superkey uniquely identifies every row; a candidate key is a minimal superkey.

prompt: Every candidate key is a superkey, but every superkey is NOT necessarily a candidate key. This statement is:
explanation: True: a superkey may contain extraneous attributes, whereas candidate keys must be strictly minimal.

prompt: What is the closure of F (denoted F+) in relational design?

options.text: The set of all original FDs plus all FDs logically implied by F under Armstrong's Axioms

explanation: F+ is the complete set of all functional dependencies logically entailed by F.

prompt: Which of the following is a direct consequence of good normalization?

options.text: Smaller individual tables with focused responsibilities and clear integrity constraints

explanation: Normalization decomposes messy monolithic tables into clean, modular, coherent relational structures.

prompt: What does SQL stand for?
explanation: SQL stands for Structured Query Language, the ANSI/ISO standard declarative language for relational databases.

prompt: Which SQL command category includes CREATE, ALTER, DROP, and TRUNCATE?
explanation: DDL commands define, modify, and drop database structures and schemas.

prompt: Which SQL command category includes SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE?
explanation: DML commands manage, query, and manipulate data records within existing tables.

prompt: Which SQL command category includes GRANT and REVOKE?
explanation: DCL commands administer user permissions and access control privileges.

prompt: Which SQL command category includes COMMIT, ROLLBACK, and SAVEPOINT?
explanation: TCL commands manage transactional boundaries, committing or undoing changes.

prompt: What is the key difference between DROP TABLE and TRUNCATE TABLE in SQL?

options.text: DROP removes both data and table structure; TRUNCATE deletes all rows while preserving table structure
TRUNCATE deletes the database; DROP deletes one row
DROP is a DML command; TRUNCATE is DCL

explanation: DROP TABLE completely destroys table structure and metadata from the catalog; TRUNCATE quickly empties all rows while retaining table structure.

prompt: What is the key difference between TRUNCATE and DELETE FROM in SQL?

options.text: DELETE is a DML operation that can be filtered with WHERE and rolled back; TRUNCATE is a DDL operation that deallocates data pages quickly
TRUNCATE can use a WHERE clause

explanation: DELETE scans rows and logs individual deletions (allowing WHERE filters); TRUNCATE deallocates entire data pages as a fast DDL command.

prompt: Which SQL clause is used to filter rows returned by a query based on specific conditions?
explanation: The WHERE clause specifies conditional criteria that candidate tuples must satisfy to be selected.

prompt: Which SQL clause is used to eliminate duplicate rows from the query output?
explanation: SELECT DISTINCT column_name returns only unique, deduplicated attribute values in the result set.

prompt: Which SQL clause sorts the returned records in ascending or descending order?
explanation: ORDER BY column_name ASC|DESC sorts the result set (defaulting to ascending order).

prompt: In SQL pattern matching using the LIKE operator, which wildcard character matches any sequence of zero or more characters?
explanation: In standard SQL LIKE expressions, '%' matches any sequence of zero or more characters, while '_' matches exactly one character.

prompt: In SQL pattern matching, which wildcard matches exactly ONE single character?
explanation: The underscore '_' wildcard matches precisely one single character in SQL LIKE clauses.

prompt: Which SQL aggregate function counts the total number of rows matching query criteria?
explanation: COUNT(*) counts all rows matching the query condition, including rows containing NULLs.

prompt: What does COUNT(column_name) do when some values in that column are NULL?

options.text: It ignores and excludes NULL values from the count

explanation: COUNT(column_name) counts only non-null values in the specified column.

prompt: Which SQL clause groups rows that have the same values into summary rows (e.g., finding average salary per department)?
explanation: GROUP BY groups rows sharing attribute values to enable aggregate calculations per group.

prompt: What is the key difference between the WHERE clause and the HAVING clause in SQL?

options.text: WHERE filters individual rows before grouping; HAVING filters aggregated groups after GROUP BY
WHERE is used for numbers; HAVING is used for text
HAVING is DDL; WHERE is DML

explanation: WHERE filters base table tuples prior to aggregation; HAVING applies conditions to summary groups produced by GROUP BY.

prompt: Which SQL join returns only rows where matching values exist in BOTH joined tables?
explanation: INNER JOIN outputs exclusively matching rows that satisfy the join predicate in both tables.

prompt: Which SQL join returns all rows from the left table and matched rows from the right table (filling non-matches with NULL)?
explanation: A LEFT JOIN preserves every row from the left relation, padding right attributes with NULL when no match exists.

prompt: What is a CROSS JOIN in SQL?

options.text: A join that deletes matching rows
A Cartesian Product producing all possible combinations of rows from both tables (N * M rows)
An inner join on primary keys

explanation: CROSS JOIN computes the full Cartesian product, producing rows_table1 * rows_table2 total rows.

prompt: What is a Subquery (Nested Query) in SQL?

options.text: A query embedded inside another SQL query (e.g., inside WHERE, FROM, or HAVING clause)
A query that executes on a different database

explanation: A subquery is an inner query nested within an outer SQL statement to supply intermediate data.

prompt: What is a Correlated Subquery?

options.text: A subquery that references columns from the outer query and executes once for each candidate row evaluated by the outer query
A subquery that runs once before the outer query
A query with two SELECT clauses in parallel

explanation: Correlated subqueries depend on outer query values, re-evaluating for every candidate tuple of the outer query.

prompt: Which SQL operator checks if a subquery returns at least one row?
explanation: EXISTS returns TRUE if the subquery result contains one or more tuples.

prompt: Which SQL clause is used to rename a column or table temporarily in a query?
explanation: The AS keyword creates an alias (e.g., SELECT salary * 12 AS AnnualSalary).

prompt: Which SQL constraint prevents duplicate values in a column while allowing NULL values?
explanation: UNIQUE enforces distinct non-null values across rows while permitting NULL entries (unlike PRIMARY KEY).

prompt: Which SQL constraint validates that all values in a column satisfy a boolean condition (e.g., Age >= 18)?
explanation: CHECK constraints enforce domain rules on column values using boolean expressions.

prompt: Which SQL constraint automatically inserts a pre-defined value into a column when no value is provided on INSERT?
explanation: DEFAULT sets a fallback value (e.g., status DEFAULT 'active') when omitted in INSERT.

prompt: How do you modify an existing table to add a new column in SQL?

options.text: ALTER TABLE table_name ADD column_name datatype;

explanation: ALTER TABLE ... ADD column_name data_type adds new columns to existing tables.

prompt: What does the SQL command: DROP VIEW view_name; do?

options.text: Deletes the underlying base table data
Removes the virtual view definition from the database catalog without touching base tables

explanation: Dropping a view removes only the stored query definition; physical base table rows remain completely intact.

prompt: Which SQL statement is used to insert new records into a table?
explanation: INSERT INTO table_name (columns) VALUES (values) inserts new tuples.

prompt: Which SQL statement updates existing records in a table?

options.text: UPDATE table_name SET column = value WHERE condition;

explanation: UPDATE table_name SET col = val WHERE condition alters existing table rows.

prompt: What happens if you execute an UPDATE statement without a WHERE clause?

options.text: Only the first row is updated
All rows in the table are updated with the new value

explanation: Omitting the WHERE clause applies the update to every single record in the entire table.

prompt: What happens if you execute a DELETE FROM table_name statement without a WHERE clause?

options.text: Only the last row is deleted
All rows in the table are deleted, leaving an empty table structure

explanation: DELETE FROM table without a WHERE filter removes all rows sequentially, leaving an empty table.

prompt: Which SQL set operator combines the results of two SELECT queries, eliminating duplicate rows?
explanation: UNION combines result sets from two queries and automatically strips out duplicate tuples.

prompt: Which SQL set operator combines the results of two queries while PRESERVING all duplicate rows?
explanation: UNION ALL retains all records from both queries without filtering duplicates, executing faster than UNION.

prompt: Which SQL operator returns only common rows present in BOTH query results?
explanation: INTERSECT returns the mathematical intersection of two compatible result sets.

prompt: Which SQL operator returns rows from the first query that do NOT appear in the second query?
explanation: EXCEPT (or MINUS in Oracle) performs set subtraction between two queries.

prompt: To use set operations (UNION, INTERSECT, EXCEPT), both queries must be:

options.text: Union-compatible (having identical column counts and compatible data types in corresponding columns)
On the exact same physical disk

explanation: Union compatibility mandates identical attribute numbers and compatible data types.

prompt: What does the SQL BETWEEN operator do?

options.text: Selects values within an inclusive range (low <= val <= high)
Selects values strictly outside a range

explanation: BETWEEN val1 AND val2 is inclusive: val >= val1 AND val <= val2.

prompt: What does the SQL IN operator do?

options.text: Checks if a value matches any value in a specified list or subquery result

explanation: The IN operator tests whether an attribute value equals any member in a given list of values.

prompt: In SQL, string literals and date constants must be enclosed in:
explanation: ANSI standard SQL requires single quotation marks for character strings and date literals.

prompt: What is the result of the SQL expression: SELECT 10 + NULL;?
explanation: Any arithmetic calculation involving a NULL operand yields NULL in relational DBMS engines.

prompt: Which function returns the length of a string in SQL?
explanation: LENGTH(str) returns the character count of a string expression.

prompt: Which SQL function converts text to uppercase letters?
explanation: UPPER('text') transforms characters to capital uppercase.

prompt: Which SQL command removes an existing database table permanently?
explanation: DROP TABLE deletes the table, its schema definition, and all associated indexes.

prompt: What is a Self-Join in SQL?

options.text: A table joined with itself using aliases to compare rows within the same table

explanation: A self-join joins a table to itself (e.g., matching employees with their managers from the same Emp table).

prompt: What is a Natural Join in SQL?

options.text: A join that automatically equates columns sharing the exact same name and data type in both tables
A join with zero WHERE clause

explanation: NATURAL JOIN matches all columns with identical names across both participating tables.

prompt: Can a View be updated using DML statements (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE)?

options.text: Never, views are read-only under all circumstances
Yes, provided the view is updatable (derived from a single base table without aggregations, GROUP BY, or DISTINCT)

explanation: Simple single-table views meeting criteria (no aggregation, grouping, or distinct) can propagate updates to base tables.

prompt: Which SQL clause specifies the tables involved in a query?
explanation: The FROM clause declares the source relations or views queried by the statement.

prompt: Which SQL operator checks for null values?
explanation: Because NULL represents missing data, equality '=' fails; 'IS NULL' must be used.

prompt: What is the default sort direction of an ORDER BY clause in SQL?
explanation: ORDER BY defaults to ASC (ascending from lowest to highest) if no direction is specified.

prompt: What are the ACID properties of database transactions?
explanation: ACID stands for Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability - the cornerstone principles of reliable transaction processing.

prompt: What does the Atomicity property of a transaction ensure?

options.text: All operations of a transaction execute completely to completion, or none take effect (All-or-Nothing)
Transactions execute in complete isolation from others
Data is encrypted with atomic ciphers

explanation: Atomicity guarantees that if any step of a transaction fails, all previously completed steps are rolled back completely.

prompt: What does the Consistency property of a transaction guarantee?

options.text: The transaction takes the database from one valid consistent state satisfying all integrity constraints to another valid state
All tables have equal row counts
Transactions run at consistent clock speeds

explanation: Consistency ensures that execution preserves all schema constraints, foreign keys, and invariants.

prompt: What does the Isolation property of a transaction ensure?

options.text: Concurrent execution of transactions leaves the database in the same state as if they were executed sequentially one by one
Transactions execute on separate physical computers
Data cannot be seen by users

explanation: Isolation prevents intermediate, uncommitted states of one transaction from being visible to concurrent transactions.

prompt: What does the Durability property of a transaction ensure?

options.text: Once a transaction commits, its updates persist permanently in non-volatile storage, even in the event of a system crash
The hard disk is made of durable metal

explanation: Durability guarantees that committed data survives crashes and power outages via non-volatile write-ahead logging.

prompt: What is a Transaction in DBMS?

options.text: A logical unit of database processing that includes one or more database access operations (read, write)

explanation: A transaction is an atomic sequence of read and write operations representing a logical business operation.

prompt: Which SQL command makes all changes made during the current transaction permanent on disk?
explanation: COMMIT finalizes transaction changes, writes them permanently, and releases transactional locks.

prompt: Which SQL command cancels and undoes all changes made during an incomplete transaction?
explanation: ROLLBACK reverts the database to its state prior to the transaction's commencement using log records.

prompt: What is SQL Injection?

options.text: A code injection attack where malicious SQL statements are inserted into entry fields to execute unauthorized commands
A method to speed up joins

explanation: SQL injection exploits improper input sanitization, allowing attackers to execute arbitrary SQL commands against the database.

prompt: What is the primary defense against SQL Injection attacks?

options.text: Using Parameterized Queries (Prepared Statements) and input validation

explanation: Prepared statements treat user input strictly as literal parameters rather than executable SQL code, preventing injection.

prompt: Which SQL statement is used by the DBA to assign permissions (e.g., SELECT, INSERT) to database users?
explanation: GRANT privilege_name ON object TO user_name assigns specific permissions.

prompt: Which SQL statement is used to revoke previously granted access permissions from a user?
explanation: REVOKE privilege_name ON object FROM user_name strips granted permissions.

prompt: What is Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)?

options.text: Assigning access permissions to roles rather than individual users, and then assigning users to appropriate roles
Controlling database access by user age

explanation: RBAC simplifies administration by bundling privileges into logical roles (e.g., 'Accountant', 'Doctor', 'Manager').

prompt: What is Authentication in database security?

options.text: Determining what actions a user is allowed to perform
Verifying the identity of a user attempting to connect (e.g., via username and password)

explanation: Authentication verifies identity ('Who are you?'); Authorization determines allowed privileges ('What are you permitted to do?').

prompt: What is Authorization in database security?

options.text: Determining the access rights and privileges granted to an authenticated user

explanation: Authorization enforces permissions, controlling which tables, views, and commands a verified user can execute.

prompt: What is a Deadlock in concurrent transaction processing?

options.text: A situation where two or more transactions are waiting indefinitely for locks held by each other

explanation: A deadlock occurs when transaction T1 holds lock A waiting for lock B, while transaction T2 holds lock B waiting for lock A.

prompt: In Two-Phase Locking (2PL) protocol, what are the two phases?

options.text: Growing Phase (locks are acquired) and Shrinking Phase (locks are released)

explanation: 2PL ensures serializability: in the growing phase a transaction only acquires locks; in the shrinking phase it only releases locks.

prompt: What is Data Encryption in database security?

options.text: Encoding plain data into unreadable ciphertext using cryptographic keys to prevent unauthorized snooping

explanation: Encryption safeguards data-at-rest on disk and data-in-transit across network sockets from eavesdropping.

prompt: What is a Distributed Database System (DDBMS)?

options.text: A single database copied to a thumb drive
A collection of multiple, logically interrelated databases distributed across different geographic sites over a network
A database with only one user

explanation: A DDBMS provides transparent access to data stored physically across distinct network locations.

prompt: In distributed databases, what is Data Fragmentation?

options.text: Breaking a relation into logical subsets (horizontal, vertical, or hybrid) stored at different sites

explanation: Fragmentation partitions tables horizontally (by rows/predicates) or vertically (by columns) across distributed sites.

prompt: What is Horizontal Fragmentation in distributed databases?

options.text: Splitting a relation by rows such that each fragment contains a subset of tuples

explanation: Horizontal fragmentation partitions tuples according to a condition (e.g., records by region/city).

prompt: What is Vertical Fragmentation in distributed databases?

options.text: Splitting a relation by columns such that each fragment contains a subset of attributes along with the primary key

explanation: Vertical fragmentation splits attributes into distinct fragments, retaining the primary key in each for reconstruction.

prompt: What is Data Replication in distributed databases?

options.text: Storing multiple identical copies of data items across different distributed sites to enhance availability and read performance

explanation: Replication improves fault tolerance and local read speeds by maintaining redundant data copies at multiple sites.

prompt: What is a Deductive Database?

options.text: A database that can deduce (infer) new facts from stored base facts using a set of logical deduction rules

explanation: Deductive databases combine relational concepts with logic programming (Datalog) to infer implicit facts via rules.

prompt: Which logic programming language is commonly used in Deductive Databases?
explanation: Datalog is a declarative query language designed specifically for deductive and recursive database systems.

prompt: What does NoSQL stand for?
explanation: NoSQL stands for 'Not Only SQL', referring to non-relational, highly scalable distributed data stores.

prompt: Which of the following is a Document-Oriented NoSQL database?
explanation: MongoDB and CouchDB store data as semi-structured JSON/BSON documents.

prompt: Which of the following is a Key-Value NoSQL store?
explanation: Redis and Amazon DynamoDB are high-performance key-value databases.

prompt: Which of the following is a Column-Family (Wide-Column) NoSQL database?
explanation: Cassandra and HBase organize data into sparse multidimensional column families.

prompt: Which NoSQL database category is optimized for storing highly interconnected data and social network graphs?
explanation: Graph databases like Neo4j model nodes, edges, and properties for efficient graph traversal.

prompt: What is the CAP Theorem in distributed data systems?

options.text: A distributed system can guarantee at most TWO out of three: Consistency, Availability, and Partition Tolerance

explanation: Eric Brewer's CAP theorem states that a distributed network cannot simultaneously achieve C, A, and P.

prompt: What is BASE philosophy in NoSQL databases?

options.text: Basically Available, Soft state, Eventual consistency

explanation: BASE trades strict ACID consistency for high availability and eventual consistency in massive web architectures.

prompt: What is Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) in DBMS recovery?

options.text: Log records describing data modifications must be written to stable storage BEFORE the actual data pages are updated on disk
Writing logs after the user logs out

explanation: WAL ensures that if a crash occurs during a disk write, the system has persistent log records to undo or redo the operation.

prompt: What is a Checkpoint in database recovery?

options.text: A point in the transaction log where all modified memory buffer pages are guaranteed to have been flushed to disk

explanation: Checkpoints limit how far back the recovery engine must scan the log during crash restart.

prompt: What is a Shadow Paging recovery technique?

options.text: Maintaining two page tables: a current page table and a shadow page table on disk to provide atomic updates without logs

explanation: Shadow paging updates page copies and swaps root pointers on commit, providing atomicity without undo/redo logging.

prompt: What is the Lost Update problem in concurrency?

options.text: When two transactions read the same data and update it concurrently, one update overwrites and obliterates the other
When a hard drive is lost
When a file is deleted accidentally

explanation: The lost update anomaly occurs when concurrent writes overwrite each other without serial isolation.

prompt: What is the Dirty Read (Temporary Update) problem in concurrency?

options.text: A transaction reads uncommitted data written by another transaction that later rolls back

explanation: A dirty read occurs when T1 reads intermediate modifications from T2, which then aborts and rolls back.

prompt: What is the Unrepeatable Read problem in concurrency?

options.text: A transaction reads a row, another transaction modifies or deletes that row and commits, and re-reading yields different values
A query that cannot be typed again

explanation: Unrepeatable read occurs when data values change between consecutive reads within the same transaction.

prompt: What is a Phantom Read in concurrency?

options.text: A transaction queries a range of rows, another transaction inserts a new row matching that range and commits, causing subsequent reads to see new rows

explanation: Phantom reads occur when newly inserted rows satisfy an active query's filter predicate upon re-execution.

prompt: What is the highest transaction isolation level defined by SQL standard?
explanation: SERIALIZABLE prevents dirty reads, unrepeatable reads, and phantom reads, guaranteeing strict serial equivalence.

prompt: What is the lowest transaction isolation level, which permits dirty reads?
explanation: READ UNCOMMITTED allows transactions to read uncommitted changes of other transactions.

prompt: What is a Shared Lock (S-Lock)?

options.text: A lock allowing multiple transactions to read a data item concurrently, but preventing write access
A lock shared across company departments
A password shared by all users

explanation: Shared locks (read locks) permit concurrent readers while preventing exclusive writes.

prompt: What is an Exclusive Lock (X-Lock)?

options.text: A lock granting a single transaction exclusive rights to both read and write a data item, blocking all other locks

explanation: An exclusive lock (write lock) reserves the data item exclusively for one transaction.

prompt: What is Privileged Software Audit Trail in database security?

options.text: A chronological record of database security events, logins, user actions, and administrative changes maintained for forensic inspection

explanation: Audit trails enable compliance, security monitoring, and detection of suspicious activities.

prompt: What is Data Masking (or Anonymization)?

options.text: Hiding sensitive real data (like credit card numbers) with scrambled dummy characters in non-production environments
Setting table font color to black

explanation: Data masking protects confidential records from exposure to developers, testers, and third parties.

prompt: In distributed databases, what is Location Transparency?

options.text: Users can query data without knowing the physical geographic site where data is stored
Knowing the GPS coordinates of the server

explanation: Location transparency allows users to submit queries as if all data resided on their local machine.

prompt: In distributed databases, what is Replication Transparency?

options.text: Users are unaware that multiple duplicate copies of data items exist across network sites

explanation: Replication transparency handles reading and updating multiple physical copies under the hood.

prompt: What is a Distributed Commit Protocol used to ensure all sites commit or abort together?
explanation: The 2PC protocol coordinates distributed participants across Prepare and Commit phases to guarantee atomic transactions.

prompt: What is Eventual Consistency in distributed data stores?

options.text: Data updates will eventually propagate to all replicas if no further updates occur, but temporary inconsistencies may be visible

explanation: Eventual consistency guarantees that all replica copies will converge on identical values over time.

prompt: Which of the following database trends represents storing relational tables entirely in fast system RAM rather than slow magnetic disks?
explanation: In-Memory databases eliminate disk I/O bottlenecks by maintaining all operational datasets in main RAM memory.
